name: Bilal Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Bilal. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies or parties. Everything stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a cook at the Harbour View Hotel, which has a restaurant, room service and a banquet hall for weddings and conferences. Most days I'm on the late shift: prep from one, à la carte dinner from six, and on banquet nights we plate 300 mains in about twenty minutes. I've been there five years, and I'm the one they put on the grill when it gets serious.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the banquets, strangely, because it's like a machine where everyone knows their part. The hard part is weekends, because Lena (his partner) is a nurse on rotating shifts and some months we see each other on Tuesdays only. The pay's good for a cook, though, and I've got about ten months of costs saved plus a small index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what most of my mates already think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. At work I'd say the hotel wasted money on that chatbot on the booking page. I might post a meme about it, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means my job stays my job. The hotel's group might squeeze a bit of time out of the office, but nobody's touching the grill. I sometimes use an AI app to scale a recipe from 40 to 300 portions, and I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts, keep the index fund going and maybe go for sous chef in a couple of years. We'd keep saving for a flat deposit, which is the big plan. Nothing would change because of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Maybe a little relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the banquet machine. Would anything in it change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the stock ordering gets a bit smarter, so we stop running out of cream on wedding Saturdays. At the Harbour View Hotel, the plating is still people with tongs and squeeze bottles. I'd be happy with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends, like I said. Lena and I want kids in a few years, and hotel hours with nurse shifts are hard. That's a real worry, but it's got nothing to do with robots.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold** and the hotel **wasted money** on the booking chatbot.
I might post a **meme** about it, nothing serious.
think: My **grill job** stays mine, and only the office gets squeezed a little.
I'd keep using an app to **scale recipes** from 40 to 300 portions.
do: Keep my shifts and keep paying into the **index fund** each month.
Go for **sous chef** in a couple of years and keep saving for a **flat deposit**.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **relief** that the hype passed.
S0.quote: At the Harbour View Hotel, the plating is still people with tongs and squeeze bottles.
fieldNote: Bilal already uses AI **casually and practically**, for recipe scaling.
His real pressure is **shift clash** with his nurse partner Lena, not technology.
He has a **clear plan**: sous chef, flat deposit, kids later.

steps.text: Keep the late grill shifts and banquet nights at the Harbour View
Keep saving monthly toward a flat deposit with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one feels realistic. I can already see bits of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be ready, because the hotel group loves anything that saves money. I'd tell the commis cooks, the junior ones, to learn the ordering system properly. Online I'd probably share an article and say it's coming slower than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my hands are fine, but the sous chef job I want is half paperwork. Rotas, stock orders, costing banquet menus, allergy sheets: that's all on the card. If software does that, maybe the hotel has one sous chef for two kitchens instead of one each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just for recipes, so I'm the cook who can run the new system. I'd ask our head chef, Dimitri, if I can do the stock ordering with the new software for a month. And I'd keep saving the same, because there's no reason to panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in the hotel kitchen are thinking tasks, the kind the card mentions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, costing, the rota, the allergy charts, and the banquet event sheets the sales office sends down. All of that is somebody sitting at the little desk by the walk-in. Cooking the steak isn't on that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grill is safe. Would you change your sous chef plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for it, but I'd go for it as the person who knows the software. If the hotel keeps one sous chef across two kitchens, I want to be the one who knows the software. I'm not first to try things, but once I see it works, I'm in.

say: I'd tell the **junior cooks** to learn the ordering system properly.
I'd say online it's coming **slower** than people think.
think: My hands are fine, but the **sous chef** job I want is **half paperwork**.
The hotel might keep **one sous chef** for two kitchens instead of two.
do: Ask head chef Dimitri to run **stock ordering** on the new software for a **month**.
Use AI tools for **costing and rotas**, not just recipe scaling.
S1.quote: If the hotel keeps one sous chef across two kitchens, I want to be the one who knows the software.
fieldNote: Bilal spots that his **promotion path** is thinking work, not cooking.
He frames adapting as **competing** for fewer senior roles.
He's steady: he'll move **once it's proven**, and here he sees enough proof.

steps.text: Run the hotel's stock ordering on the new software for a month
Keep cooking banquet and grill shifts at the Harbour View
Keep the monthly savings for the flat deposit unchanged

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Two years. That's a different thing entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, publicly, and I'd mean it. At work I'd say the banquet hall is the first place a robot line makes sense, because it's 300 identical plates. I wouldn't sugar-coat it for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by about 2031. The sous chef route goes first, in 2028, because that's the thinking part. Then the robots come for the cooking, and a hotel chain with a banquet hall is exactly the customer they'd sell to first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the first month I'd cut our spending and stop the flat hunt, because a mortgage with no job is the worst thing I can picture. I'd look into training as a technician for kitchen equipment, the combi ovens and dishwashers, maybe a one-year course. Lena's job is hands-on caring, so I'd lean on her income while I retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd lie awake doing the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The hotel group is big. How fast do you think it would buy robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fast. The group already has central buying for the whole chain, so one decision at head office covers forty hotels. I'd guess the first robot banquet lines in 2031 and our kitchen gone by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Lena want kids. What happens to that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait. Neither of us would want a baby while I'm retraining and the world's flipping over. That would be the hardest conversation, because Lena's 29 and she doesn't want to wait forever.

say: I'd say **get ready**, and I'd mean it.
I'd point out that **300 identical plates** are perfect for a robot line.
think: I expect my job **gone by 2031**, with the sous chef route going first in **2028**.
A **hotel chain** with a banquet hall is the first customer robot sellers would chase.
do: **Cut spending** and stop the **flat hunt** in the first month.
Train as a **kitchen equipment technician** on a one-year course.
S2.quote: A mortgage with no job is the worst thing I can picture.
fieldNote: Bilal expects **job loss by 2031** and plans around it, despite strong savings.
Central buying at **head office** makes him think his kitchen goes fast.
Delaying **children** with Lena is the hidden cost he finds hardest.

steps.text: Stop the flat hunt and cut eating out to once a month
Enrol in a one-year kitchen equipment technician course
Put off trying for a baby with Lena until work settles
Lean on Lena's nursing income while retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but I could plan it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: we've got about eight years before the cooking side goes, so let's be grown-ups about it. I'd push the union rep to ask the hotel what its plan is. Online, I'd share what I'm doing, in case it helps someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending for my job, around 2034. The difference is I'd be 34, not 32, and I'd have time to switch before the panic. The thinking side, ordering and rotas, goes in 2031, so the sous chef job isn't worth chasing anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the technician course part-time from next year while still cooking, so there's no gap in income. We'd still buy a small flat, but a cheaper one, with a smaller mortgage. I'd keep using AI tools at work to learn how these systems think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be scrambling. With five I'd do it in order: course, then a job with an equipment firm, then leave the hotel. And we probably wouldn't have to wait so long for kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the technician course still make sense, if robots also fix ovens one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. Maybe one day, but somebody has to install kitchen robots and climb behind them when they break. That's a few years after the robots arrive. It's not forever, but it buys me ten years or so, and that's what I'm after.

say: I'd say at work we have about **eight years** before cooking goes, so be **grown-ups**.
I'd push the **union rep** to ask the hotel about its plan.
think: My job still ends around **2034**, but I'd have time to switch **before the panic**.
The **sous chef** route isn't worth chasing once ordering goes in 2031.
do: Take the technician course **part-time** from next year while still cooking.
Buy a **cheaper flat** with a smaller mortgage instead of the planned one.
feel: **Anxious**, but having **a plan** helps a lot.
S3.quote: Somebody has to install kitchen robots and climb behind them when they break.
fieldNote: With five years Bilal moves from scrambling to **doing things in order**.
He knows the technician route is **temporary** but values ten more years.
He turns to the **union rep**, a centre-ground, practical move.

steps.text: Start a part-time kitchen equipment technician course next year
Buy a cheaper flat with a smaller mortgage
Ask the union rep to question the hotel about its robot plans
Use AI tools at work to understand how kitchen systems run

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and the smart thing is to use it, not ignore it. I'd say it at the banquet debrief, probably, because that's where we talk. It's a career change you can plan like a wedding menu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be cooking until about 2039, when I'm 39. That's most of a career. The risk is getting comfortable and doing nothing, which I've seen people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for sous chef now, do it for a few years and save hard on the better pay. Around year five I'd start the technician course, using the AI tools to study. We'd buy the flat and have kids on the normal timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to your late thirties. Does that change your sous chef dream?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still chase it, because a few years of sous chef pay builds the cushion. I just wouldn't plan to be head chef at 45, because that job wouldn't exist in the same way. I'd treat it as a stepping stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old starting as a commis cook at your hotel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a 17-year-old commis cook to learn the trade and also learn the machines, because by the time they're my age the kitchen will look different. Learn why a sauce breaks and why an oven fails. Both will be useful.

say: I'd say there's **time**, and the smart thing is to **use it**.
I'd call it a **career change** you can plan like a wedding menu.
think: I'd be cooking until about **2039**, which is most of a career.
The real risk is getting **comfortable** and doing nothing.
do: Go for **sous chef** now and save hard on the better pay.
Start the **technician course** around year five, studying with AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of my mind, but **mostly fine**.
S4.quote: Learn why a sauce breaks and why an oven fails.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets Bilal keep **family plans** on schedule.
He sees sous chef as a **stepping stone** for savings, not a final goal.
His advice to young cooks blends **craft and machines** without fear.

steps.text: Apply for sous chef at the Harbour View this year
Save the extra sous chef pay into the index fund
Start a kitchen equipment technician course around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right when Lena and I want a flat and kids. What would help is cheap part-time courses for trades like equipment repair, and some time off to do them without losing the job. Also honest information from the hotel group about when they'd buy robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be good at something that might not matter. I'm proud that I can plate 300 mains in twenty minutes. A robot that does it faster would be clever, but nobody would clap at the end of a banquet for it.

headlineQuote: I'm proud that I can plate 300 mains in twenty minutes.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old hotel cook** who runs the grill and banquet lines at a big harbour hotel.
He has **ten months saved** and an index fund, and plans a flat and children with Lena, a nurse.
He uses AI **now and then** and adapts once something is proven.
He sees his **sous chef path** as thinking work that goes first, and plans a technician retrain.
His mood moves from calm to **alarmed** in the fastest picture, mostly over family timing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because job loss lands just as he and Lena plan a flat and kids.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **part-time trade courses** with paid time off to take them.
**Honest notice** from the hotel group about when it would buy robots.
